title: Here's what actually happened when someone asked it a simple question.
description:
Here's what actually happened when someone asked it a simple question. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson asked Eugene Goostman how many legs an ant has.

That was the chatbot's actual answer. It never answered a single one of Aaronson's questions directly, deflecting each one with jokes and topic changes instead.

Built Goostman as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy with a pet guinea pig, a gynaecologist father, and a built-in excuse for every grammar mistake it made.

A modified Cleverbot had already beaten that in 2011. At the Techniche festival that year, Cleverbot convinced 59.3% of a much larger voting pool, under the same 30% pass threshold Turing had suggested.

Imperial College AI professor Murray Shanahan called the 'pass' claim 'completely misplaced', saying it devalues real AI research.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Goostman: confirms the 2001 creation by Vladimir Veselov, Eugene Demchenko and Sergey Ulasen, the 13-year-old Ukrainian persona from Odesa with a pet guinea pig and a gynaecologist father, the 7 June 2014 Royal Society event organised by Kevin Warwick with 33% of 30 judges convinced, the 2011 Techniche festival result for a modified Cleverbot (59.3% of 1,334 votes), and Murray Shanahan's 'completely misplaced' quote.
- http://www.scottaaronson.com/blog/?p=1858: Scott Aaronson's own blog post transcribing his full conversation with Eugene Goostman, including the ant-leg exchange quoted directly.
